meta.title: Who really said "We're more popular than Jesus now; I don't know which will go first — rock and roll or Christianity"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: John Lennon really said it — to Maureen Cleave, London Evening Standard, 4 March 1966. The full article confirms the wording. "Bigger than Jesus" is the paraphrase.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'We're more popular than Jesus now; I don't know which will go first — rock and roll or Christianity'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine John Lennon, verbatim, from Maureen Cleave's Evening Standard profile of 4 March 1966 — not a boast, and not "bigger than Jesus."

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: 1940–1980 · English singer-songwriter, co-founder of the Beatles
answer.sourceLine: Lennon said it to journalist Maureen Cleave at his Weybridge home, and it ran in her profile “How Does a Beatle Live? John Lennon Lives Like This” in the London Evening Standard on 4 March 1966. The full article — reprinted by permission of the Evening Standard — carries the sentence word for word, and Wikiquote files it in its sourced section, not among the disputed.

source.heading: The interview

docMeta.dd: How Does a Beatle Live? John Lennon Lives Like This

source.excerpt: Experience has sown few seeds of doubt in him: not that his mind is closed, but it’s closed round whatever he believes at the time. “Christianity will go,” he said. “It will vanish and shrink. I needn’t argue about that; I’m right and I will be proved right. We’re more popular than Jesus now; I don’t know which will go first—rock ’n’ roll or Christianity. Jesus was all right, but his disciples were thick and ordinary. It’s them twisting it that ruins it for me.” He is reading extensively about religion.
trail: Started with the specialists. Quote Investigator has no entry on this line, but Wikiquote carries it in its sourced Quotes section ↗ — not under Disputed or Misattributed — citing Maureen Cleave’s interview in London’s Evening Standard of 4 March 1966.

Then went to the article itself. A scholarly documents appendix reproduces the complete profile, credited “from London Evening Standard, March 4, 1966. Reprinted by permission of the Evening Standard” ↗. The sentence appears there exactly as quoted, inside a longer passage about Christianity.

Cross-checked the framing. Wikipedia’s account of the controversy ↗ confirms the 4 March 1966 publication, the secondary heading “On a hill in Surrey … A young man, famous, loaded, and waiting for something,” and that the widely used “bigger than Jesus” is not what Lennon said.
Followed it forward. The Datebook reprint ↗ and the Chicago press conference of 11 August 1966 ↗ document how the sentence detached from its paragraph and became an international incident.
source.excerptNote: Taken from the complete article as reprinted by permission of the Evening Standard. Note that the printed text reads “rock ’n’ roll” and uses a dash where many reproductions use a comma — the substance is unchanged.

author.bio: Born in Liverpool on 9 October 1940, Lennon co-founded the Beatles and, with Paul McCartney, wrote one of the most-covered songbooks in popular music. He was 25 when Maureen Cleave spent a day with him for the Evening Standard — bored in a mock-Tudor house in the stockbroker belt, reading extensively about religion, and, as Cleave put it, with a mind “closed round whatever he believes at the time.” He was shot dead in New York on 8 December 1980.

misattribution.heading: What goes wrong with this one
misattribution.intro: The attribution is right — this is one of the rare famous-name quotes that survives checking intact. What travels badly is the wording and the meaning.

items.why: The form almost everyone repeats. Wikipedia’s account of the affair notes that “bigger than Jesus” has been used in analysis of the controversy, but Lennon’s words were “more popular than Jesus” ↗. “Bigger” sounds like a boast; “more popular” was an observation about audience size.

items.who: A claim that the Beatles outranked Christ
items.why: Both speaker and journalist rejected this. Cleave said “John was certainly not comparing The Beatles with Christ” ↗ but observing how weak Christianity had become; Lennon, in Chicago on 11 August 1966 ↗, said he had used “Beatles” as a remote example and could have said television instead.

items.who: An outburst on the 1966 American tour
items.why: It was said quietly at home in Weybridge and printed in London on 4 March 1966, to almost no reaction. The firestorm came months later, when the American teen magazine Datebook put half the sentence on its September 1966 cover ↗.
A harmless house-style difference, worth knowing if you are quoting precisely: the Evening Standard text prints “rock ’n’ roll” ↗, while many reproductions, including Wikiquote, spell it out.

misattribution.truthLine: Lennon said it, in these words, to Maureen Cleave — and the sentence is printed verbatim in her Evening Standard article of 4 March 1966 ↗. It is the paraphrase — and the reading — that are wrong, not the attribution.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The remark caused almost nothing in Britain. It ran on a Friday in March 1966 in a chatty profile about a rich 25-year-old who couldn’t remember what day it was, and British readers — in a country where church attendance was already sliding — largely shrugged. The sentence only became a scandal when it crossed the Atlantic stripped of the paragraph around it.

In its September 1966 issue, which reached American media on 29 July, the teen magazine Datebook put the second half of the line on its cover: “I don’t know which will go first — rock ’n’ roll or Christianity.” Southern radio stations organised record burnings, the Ku Klux Klan picketed, and on 11 August 1966 Lennon sat in front of the cameras at Chicago’s Astor Tower Hotel and apologised. The Beatles played their last commercial concert in San Francisco on 29 August 1966.
detailsBody: At the Chicago press conference he unpicked his own sentence: “I used the word ‘Beatles’ as a remote thing — not as what ‘I’ think as Beatles — as those other Beatles like other people see us. I just said ‘they’ are having more influence on kids and things than anything else, including Jesus. But I said it that way which is the wrong way.”

Cleave herself defended the reading: “John was certainly not comparing the Beatles with Christ. He was simply observing that so weak was the state of Christianity that the Beatles were, to many people, better known.” She added that he had intended to be ironic.
context.pull: “If I had said television is more popular than Jesus, I might have got away with it.”
